Tiller
TIL-ur
n. (one who cultivates the ground; the trade of Cain)
From Old English tilian, to strive after, to cultivate — the same root as till in the sense of labour. It renders Hebrew oved adamah, a server of the ground, from abad, to work or serve, and adamah, the ground from which Adam was taken.

Biblical Definition

And she again bare his brother Abel. And Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground. Two trades, introduced in a single verse, and the text gives no hint that one is better. Tilling was the first commission — there was not a man to till the ground before Adam was made, and when the man was driven out of Eden it was to till the ground from whence he was taken. Cain took up his father's work. What went wrong was not the trade but the offering, and the New Testament says why: by faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain. Then the ground itself became the instrument of the sentence. God, who had cursed the ground for Adam's sake, tells Cain: When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth. The tiller is sentenced to till soil that will not answer him. From that point Scripture treats the ground as a witness — the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground — and the curse stands over all human labour until the last Adam, buried in the earth, comes out of it in a garden.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one who tills; a husbandman; a cultivator; one who ploughs or cultivates the earth.

expand to see more

TILLER, n. One who tills; a husbandman; a cultivator.

TILL, v.t. To labor; to cultivate; to plow and prepare for seed, and to dress crops.

TILLAGE, n. The operation, practice or art of tilling and preparing land for seed, and keeping the ground free from weeds.

HUSBANDMAN, n. A farmer; a cultivator or tiller of the ground.

VAGABOND, n. A vagrant; one who wanders from town to town without any settled habitation.

Key Scripture

Genesis 4:2 — "And she again bare his brother Abel. And Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground."

Genesis 2:5 — "And every plant of the field before it was in the earth, and every herb of the field before it grew: for the LORD God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was not a man to till the ground."

Genesis 3:23 — "Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken."

Genesis 4:12 — "When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth."

Modern Corruption

Work is treated either as a curse to be escaped or as the source of a man's worth; Genesis gives tillage before the fall as a commission and after it as a labour under a curse, and neither reading survives the text.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors about work both misread Genesis 2 and 3. The first says labour is a consequence of the fall, something to be minimized and finally escaped — a view that makes retirement the goal of life and treats the working years as a sentence served. But Adam was put in the garden to dress it and to keep it before there was any sin in the world; the commission is older than the curse. What the fall introduced was thorns, sweat, frustration and a ground that does not answer honest effort. The work itself was a gift, and remains one.

The second error makes a man's work his identity, so that his value rises and falls with his output. Cain is the warning here. His offering was of the fruit of the ground — his own labour, brought to God — and when it was not respected he was wroth and his countenance fell, and God asked him why. A man whose worth is his yield has no answer when the yield fails, and the ground had already been told not to give Cain its strength. Paul settles the question for Christians from another direction entirely: whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men; knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew abad (H5647), to work, serve, till; adamah (H127), the ground; Qayin (H7014), Cain; arar (H779), to curse.

expand to see more

Hebrew abad (H5647) — to work or serve; the same verb for tilling soil and for serving God.

Hebrew adamah (H127) — the ground; the word from which Adam is taken, and to which he returns.

Hebrew koach (H3581) — strength; the ground shall not yield Cain her strength.

Hebrew arar (H779) — to curse; the ground cursed for Adam's sake, and Cain cursed from the ground.

Hebrew na and nad (H5128) — a fugitive and a vagabond; the sentence on the first tiller who shed blood.

Usage

"“Cain was a tiller of the ground” — his father's trade, taken up without comment."

"“there was not a man to till the ground” — the commission older than the curse."

"“it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength” — the sentence laid in the soil."
